title: Adaptive acoustic comfort: Evidence from an acoustic neutrality approach in naturally ventilated office buildings
authors_and_source: Yuksel Dicle S.,Aletta F., Kang J. Applied Acoustics, 257, 111627
abstract: Acoustic comfort is commonly assessed using fixed sound-level criteria that assume stable exposure–response relationships. However, in naturally ventilated buildings, occupants’ evaluations may vary with changing acoustic exposure and adaptive responses. Although such adaptive relationships are well established in thermal comfort research, they remain underexplored in acoustics. This study examines an adaptive perspective on acoustic comfort assessment through a field study conducted in six naturally ventilated or mixed-mode open-plan offices involving 72 participants and 480 observations. Repeated in situ perceptual evaluations, concurrent indoor and outdoor sound- level measurements, and self-reported adaptive behaviours were collected and analysed using mixed-effects modelling approaches. For level-based evaluations, an Acoustic Sensation Vote (ASV) of 0 (“neither loud nor quiet”) emerged as the operational acoustic neutral reference, representing a threshold-like transition to dissatisfaction. Office-specific neutral levels ranged from 47.2 to 53.3 dB and tended to be higher in offices with higher indoor sound- level exposure. Adaptive actions were more likely at higher preceding-hour indoor L (OR = 1.55 per 5 dB), and observations with reported adaptive behaviour were slightly more quiet-oriented after accounting for concurrent indoor sound level and office. Outdoor L did not provide additional explanatory information for ASV; however, among neutral evaluations, each 1-dB increase in outdoor L was associated with an approximately 0.16-dB increase in concurrent indoor sound level. Overall, the findings provide empirical support for a context-sensitive adaptive acoustic comfort perspective in which acoustic evaluations are considered in relation to indoor exposure, office context, behavioural responses and outdoor acoustic conditions. The findings should be interpreted within the scope of six London offices and a field-based design in which acoustic and contextual conditions could not be fully standardised across participants. For office design and assessment, the results suggest that fixed sound-level criteria can be complemented by consideration of office-specific acoustic exposure and occupants’ opportunities for behavioural adjustment, particularly in naturally ventilated workplaces.

title: Thermal resilience and well-being in Alpine social housing under heatwave conditions: a mixed-methods study for climate-adaptive retrofit
authors_and_source: Paoletti G.,Gupta A., Carnelli F.,Toledo L., Babich F. Energy and Buildings , 374, 118442
abstract: Climate change is intensifying heatwaves in cold-climate regions, increasing indoor overheating risks for vulnerable groups, including elderly and low-income residents in social housing. Evidence on thermal resilience and climate- adaptive retrofit for Alpine social housing remains limited, particularly at dwelling scale and under real occupancy conditions. This study investigates indoor overheating as both measured exposure and lived experience in twelve social housing apartments in Casette Inglesi district of Bolzano, Italy, during summer 2024. A mixed-methods Aeq Aeq Aeq approach combined indoor environmental monitoring, architectural survey, and resident interviews on perceived comfort and heat-related well-being, adaptive practices, and constraints. Over valid monitored periods, time above EN 16798–1 Category II adaptive comfort threshold ranged from 0% to 47.48%, reaching 99.74% during July heatwave in a west-facing upper-floor living room beneath an uninsulated pitched roof, despite window replacement and reported A/C use in an adjacent room. Interviews showed that residents relied on multiple adaptive strategies, including daytime window closure, shading, cross-ventilation, fans, and A/C. However, their practical applicability varied due to health conditions, energy-cost concerns, limited control over building-level interventions, comfort preferences, and non-thermal constraints such as outdoor noise, mosquitoes, and safety concerns. Prioritised interventions ranged from external shading, insect screens, and fans to envelope improvements and accessibility upgrades. Findings suggest that overheating risk in Alpine social housing is shaped not only by envelope performance, but also by the interaction between dwelling exposure, adaptive opportunities, resident vulnerability, and institutional feasibility. The study proposes a transferable mixed-methods approach for identifying evidence- informed retrofit priorities in vulnerable Alpine social housing.

title: Exploring interactions of thermal, acoustic, and aesthetic environments on thermal experience in parks
authors_and_source: Zhang Y.,Uchiyama Y., Sato M. Scientific Reports, 16(1), 8564
abstract: The thermal comfort of urban parks is crucial for residents’ well-being and urban livability. There is limited research on the integration of different environmental factors in urban parks, with most studies focusing on hot, sunny days in summer. This study explored the interactions of multi-sensory factors, including thermal, acoustic, and aesthetic, on thermal experience in parks across various weather types. The results reveal that thermal conditions directly dominate thermal experience. Acoustic comfort has a relatively weak positive effect on thermal comfort, and this effect disappears under strong heat-stress conditions. Natural sounds help increase thermal acceptability, whereas mechanically dominated soundscapes have the opposite effect. Aesthetic satisfaction also contributes to higher thermal acceptability. Compared with blue spaces, aesthetic satisfaction with green spaces exerts a more consistently positive influence on thermal experience. The negative effect of PET is significantly weaker than the positive effects of perceived acoustic comfort and aesthetic satisfaction on overall satisfaction. The revealed multi-sensory interactions yield practical recommendations for urban planners and designers in addressing climate change and enhancing urban livability.

title: Evaluation of heat stress mitigation potentials of climate change adaptation measures in cities: Scenario analyses for technical- and nature-based solutions using 3D microclimate modelling
authors_and_source: Eingruber N., Zimmermann D., Korres W.,Lohnert U., Schneider K. Climate Risk Management , 54, 100894
abstract: Urban areas are expected to warm significantly more than the global average according to climate projections. This will lead to many adverse effects such as increasing health risks and mortality rates, making climate change adaptation crucial for future urban planning. Identifying effective and suitable adaptation measures requires assessment of cooling potentials, societal acceptance and cost effectiveness based on sound-scientific analyses. High-resolution microclimate modelling and scenario analyses are a promising approach to evaluate thermal effects of climate adaptation measures. A physically-based 3D-gridded ENVI-met model was parameterized based on field measurements and remote sensing data to simulate the microclimate of a 16-ha urban high-density area in Cologne/Germany. The model was successfully validated using a densely-distributed NETATMO sensor network in the study area. We evaluated 92 adaptation scenarios for a 20-year extreme heat event to quantify heat mitigation potentials. Scenarios included technical- and nature-based solutions at buildings as well as in street corridors. Measures were simulated individually and in combinations, across varying idealized and more realistic implementation degrees. Results showed a significant mean air temperature reduction by -3.0 K up to -6.3 K as well as significant mean cooling effects on physiological equivalent temperature (PET) of -4.3 K up to -11.1 K in pedestrian height level, particularly for scenarios with high greenery coverage. Combinations of different nature-based and technical solutions performed better than single measures. Even partial implementations (e.g., 25% greened buildings) provided significant cooling effects in the entire quarter, while high-reflective surfaces and shading structures had limited impact on thermal outdoor comfort.

title: Environmental regulation of sunken courtyards in standalone underground spaces: field measurements and ventilation-oriented design strategies
authors_and_source: Wen Y.,Ouyang M., Wang Y.,... Guo T.,Wei H. Tunnelling and Underground Space Technology , 178, 108030
abstract: While sunken courtyards are widely recognised for enhancing underground environmental quality, modern architectural practices frequently prioritise aesthetic and circulation. This deficiency is critical in standalone underground spaces, where the absence of adjacent aboveground massing restricts wind pressure differentials and downdraughts. Using a standalone underground museum as a case study, this research correlates early design strategies with post-construction field measurements to evaluate compliance with wind, thermal, acoustic, and air- quality regulations. Furthermore, Computational Fluid Dynamics simulations are utilised to analyse the aerodynamic impact of courtyard morphology on natural ventilation. The study identifies an optimal length-to-depth (L/D) ratio of 1.5, balancing ventilation performance with land-use efficiency. However, under low ambient wind conditions, supplementary strategies are necessary to enhance underground natural ventilation, thereby elevating average indoor and outdoor wind velocities to approximately 0.380 m/s and 0.650 m/s, respectively. Consequently, this research quantitatively verifies the efficacy of spatial loops, windcatchers, and wind deflectors. Results demonstrate that spatial loops significantly enhance natural ventilation by enriching the distribution of pressure differentials and facilitating global cross-ventilation. Conversely, windcatchers and wind deflectors only offer moderate enhancements for sunken wells (L/D = 0.5), while exerting attenuation effects or negligible impacts on the sunken courtyard (L/D = 1.5), such as a paradoxical 34.44 % reduction in indoor wind velocity caused by aerodynamic conflicts. These findings facilitate the design transition towards open morphology and performance integration, both of which are essential for modern underground spaces.

title: Assessing impacts of human activity on indoor air pollutants using noise and CO2-based variables with LSTM-LightGBM: a library case study
authors_and_source: Zhang H.,Srinivasan R., Chen C.,... Ganesan V., Zhou R. Atmospheric Environment , 385, 122350
abstract: This study demonstrates the limitations of using carbon dioxide (CO ) alone as a proxy for human activity intensity in multi-pollutant indoor air quality modeling. In a university library, an integrated indoor–outdoor monitoring system collected two weeks of continuous measurements of CO , noise, temperature, relative humidity, PM . , PM , CO, O , NO , SO , and eTVOCs. A hybrid time-series framework combining long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) was developed to compare six feature-set scenarios based on different combinations of CO , noise, temperature, and relative humidity. Association analysis and feature extraction showed that the combined CO , noise, temperature, and relative humidity factors had markedly stronger relationships with most indoor pollutants than CO or noise alone (R = 0.59–0.91, p < 0.05). CO was more informative for particulate matter, whereas noise was better suited to several gaseous pollutants. Validation with the LSTM–LightGBM framework supported these results. Beyond the general benefit of adding predictors, leave-one-predictor-out ablation comparisons indicated pollutant-specific and partially non-redundant predictor roles. Noise provided 2 2 2 5 10 3 2 2 2 2 2 2 independent information beyond CO for NO , CO, and eTVOCs, whereas temperature and relative humidity primarily improved prediction through interactions with activity-related proxies rather than serving as universally informative variables. The full-variable model is therefore interpreted as a reference upper-bound scenario, while the main finding is that pollutant prediction depends on distinct combinations of CO , noise, and thermo-hygrometric variables, without implying direct causal effects of human activity. These results provide a practical basis for improving feature engineering and indoor air quality control in similar built environments.

title: Robust Thermal Stability, Flame Retardancy, and Weather Resistance Cross-Linked Cellulose Aerogel toward High-Performance Passive Radiative Cooling
authors_and_source: Zhao Z.,Zhu S.,Zhang C., ... Li Z.,Wu X. ACS Applied Materials and Interfaces , 18(43)
abstract: The frequent occurrence of high temperatures has driven the development of green passive cooling technologies. Traditional passive radiative cooling materials have single performance, insufficient weather resistance and structural stability, and are unable to adapt to outdoor multifunctional thermal management. In this study, cellulose nanofibers were used as the substrate, and silica and methyltrimethoxysilane were incorporated to prepare a composite aerogel. Tests show that the optimal sample has excellent radiation cooling, heat insulation, flame retardancy, hydrophobicity, and sound absorption performance. With a solar reflectance of 93.5% and a mid-infrared emissivity of 94.3%, it provides a maximum outdoor temperature reduction of 15.7 °C. Its minimum thermal conductivity reaches 0.034 W m K , offering excellent thermal insulation performance. The total heat release and the rate of heat release were significantly reduced, and flame retardancy was greatly improved. In addition, the sample exhibits a water contact angle of 137.2°, endowing it with favorable self-cleaning properties. The average sound absorption coefficient reaches 0.78 in the broadband range of 1000–6300 Hz, and the noise reduction performance is superior to that of commercial materials. This multifunctional composite aerogel overcomes the performance limitations of traditional materials and offers new insights into the development and application of outdoor integrated thermal management functional materials.

title: Numerical simulation and experimental comparison of strain measurements within a vertical bifacial photovoltaic noise barrier demonstrator
authors_and_source: Casasola M.,Engelen T., Kyranaki N., ... Poortmans J.,Daenen M. Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells , 305, 114438
abstract: A photovoltaic noise barrier (PVNB) is an example of infrastructure-integrated photovoltaics (IIPV) that serves as a conventional roadside infrastructure element while also generating solar energy. These integrated applications of photovoltaic (PV) modules are particularly relevant in areas where there is limited land area available for the installation of PV plants. Like any engineering structure, a PVNB is influenced by environmental factors such as temperature variations, wind loads and other external stressors. This study focuses on temperature fluctuations and the resulting thermomechanical strains within a PVNB demonstrator in Genk, Belgium. To achieve this, optical fibre Bragg grating (FBG) sensors for temperature and strain monitoring are implemented within the PV modules on the inner surface of the glass cover at three different locations. Both the trend of increases and decreases in monitored temperatures and strains are in good agreement with the data recorded by a nearby meteorological station. Subsequently, numerical simulations are performed and compared with the experimentally measured values, demonstrating a strong correlation with only one stressor input, i.e. the monitored temperature within the PV modules. Furthermore, the influence of using alternative encapsulant materials, such as thermoplastic polyolefin (TPO) or polyvinyl butyral (PVB) instead of the more commonly used ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA), on the strains and stress distributions on the cells is studied. This work proves, therefore, the possibility of real-time monitoring of internal strains within PV-integrated outdoor applications and strengthens the use of numerical simulations in forecasting internal stresses for the use in degradation models.

title: A framework for assessing smart thermostat fault detection and diagnosis under unmeasurable building load disturbances
authors_and_source: Ejenakevwe K.A., Tiamiyu N.,Hurt R., Wang G.,Song L. Energy and Buildings , 368, 117856
abstract: Smart thermostat-based fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) for residential air-conditioning (AC) systems is gaining traction due to its low-cost prospect. However, smart thermostats measure only a limited set of variables, raising concerns about the reliability and applicability of thermostat-driven FDD. This study therefore proposes a representative co-simulation testbed and six quantitative performance metrics for assessing smart thermostat FDD methods. The testbed integrates models of a residential building, a vapor compression AC system, and unmeasurable building load disturbances (UBLD) arising from occupant behavior and weather variability. For representativeness, a co-simulation approach was used with EnergyPlus for building modeling and a Dymola for AC modeling. Additionally, components from three specialized Modelica-based libraries were used to develop the testbed, making it more representative. To demonstrate the testbed's capability to capture UBLDs due to irregular occupancy patterns and/or weather conditions (e.g., windspeed and outdoor temperature), 15 case studies of faults and UBLDs were designed and simulated. The UBLD scenarios were designed from two survey data. Simulation results were then used to analyze the impact of UBLDs and common AC faults on FDD performance. The analyses show that UBLDs could cause false alarm rates of up to 30% even with a 15% deviation threshold, and that this can be reduced with a cumulative sum (CUSUM) logic. Furthermore, a signal-to-noise ratio metric – incorporating both false positive and false negative rates – is applied to assess a commonly used FDD feature, duty factor, and revealed its limited effectiveness. Overall, this study demonstrates the value of the proposed co-simulation testbed and evaluation metrics for assessing the performance and limitations of smart thermostat-based data-driven FDD methods in residential AC systems.

title: Material Selection for Components of an On- Campus Study Pod
authors_and_source: Odah E.,Abdullah R., Alsswey A.,Mostafa A. Jordan Journal of Civil Engineering , 20(4)
abstract: On-campus study pods offer private, flexible learning spaces designed to provide controlled thermal and acoustic environments within busy university settings. This study presents a systematic material selection process for the key components of a compact, modular, weather-exposed study pod designed for 2–4 students. Using the Ashby methodology, six application-specific performance indices were derived to optimize stiffness-to-weight, strength-to- weight, wear resistance, thermal insulation, thermal expansion compatibility, and cost efficiency. Realistic design constraints, including self-weight, occupancy loads, wind pressure, and deflection limits, were applied alongside outdoor durability, acoustic comfort, and sustainability requirements. The optimal materials identified are 5000-series aluminium alloys for the structural frame, a multilayer sandwich configuration (treated softwood/bamboo outer layer, rigid polyurethane foam core, and cork inner layer) for enclosure panels, plywood and polypropylene for seating and desks, and treated bamboo/plywood with polycarbonate options for roofing. Quantitative comparisons demonstrate approximately 42% mass reduction for the aluminium frame versus stainless steel, and 3–5 times lower heat transfer for cork/PU foam panels compared with untreated wood. The selected materials balance structural performance, thermal and acoustic comfort, recyclability, and economic feasibility while supporting circular-economy principles. Limitations and future validation pathways, including finite element analysis and prototype testing, are discussed.

title: Dynamic turbulence modeling with experimental validation over a 13-km free- space optical link
authors_and_source: Ge H.,Song Y.,an Y., Wang T.,Dong K. Optics Express, 34(18)
abstract: To evaluate atmospheric turbulence impacts on free-space optical (FSO) communications, this paper generates dynamic phase screens via the covariance matrix method (CMM) and the time-delay-induced autoregressive (TDI-AR) model to simulate the turbulence channel. Concurrently, a log-frequency weighted least squares (LF-WLS) inversion method is constructed to extract simulation parameters (transverse wind speed v and decorrelation time τ ) from temporal power spectra. Numerical simulations verify the spatiotemporal statistics of the generated phase screens and the accuracy of parameter inversion, after which the system reliability and channel fading characteristics are analyzed. Comparisons with a 13-km outdoor FSO experiment show good agreement in the statistical properties of the received power. For the 1.25-Gb/s link, the simulations employed a fixed equivalent SNR and captured the relative BER variation observed experimentally under different turbulence conditions. This research provides a theoretical and numerical basis for FSO channel modeling and performance evaluation under complex atmospheric conditions.

title: A Physical Environment Evaluation System for Outdoor Sports Spaces in Urban Residential Areas of a Severe Cold-Region City: A Case Study of Harbin, China
authors_and_source: Xia S.,Luo P.,Liu X.,Wang T. Buildings, 16(18), 3762
abstract: Outdoor sports spaces in residential areas must provide safe and comfortable conditions for daily exercise, yet in severe cold regions their use is constrained by wind, solar exposure, thermal stress, noise, and air quality. Using six sites in Harbin, China, this study developed an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)-based evaluation system covering the wind, light, acoustic, thermal, and air environments. Candidate indicators were screened using a user questionnaire, expert AHP judgments were used to derive weights, and site performance was quantified through field monitoring, site surveys, and ENVI-met simulation. The indicator weights, in descending order, were wet-bulb globe temperature (14.96%), pedestrian-level wind speed (13.67%), building layout conducive to air circulation (13.55%), pedestrian-level wind vortices and still-air zones (12.79%), sunlight exposure and lighting effectiveness (12.67%), shading rate of hard ground surfaces and structures (12.15%), reflectivity of pavement and covering materials (11.37%), and outdoor noise level (8.83%). Overall scores differed across the six sites. An AHP-weighted performance-shortfall analysis, calculated relative to the ideal Grade 5, identified outdoor noise, shading, building-layout-related air circulation, and sunlight/lighting performance as the four largest cross-site improvement needs. The resulting framework supports the diagnosis and renewal of outdoor sports spaces in cold-region residential areas. The empirical results represent the monitored summer and autumn transitional scenarios rather than year-round performance.

title: Hybrid Thermal-Compensated State Motion Detection Adaptive Kalman Filter for Error Suppression in Low-Cost MEMS IMU
authors_and_source: Zeng X.,Tong Q.,Gao F., ... Xing F.,You Z. IEEE Sensors Journal, 26(18)
abstract: Low-cost microelectromechanical system (MEMS) inertial measurement units (IMUs) have gained widespread adoption across diverse application domains; however, their application in precision-demanding scenarios remains limited by stochastic errors and thermal-induced drift. To mitigate these limitations, this article first establishes a unified stochastic error model for accelerometers and gyroscopes and subsequently proposes a hybrid error suppression framework designated as the thermal-compensated state motion detection adaptive Kalman filter (TC- SMD AKF). The polynomial fitting-based temperature compensation eliminates drift-induced filtering misjudgment, while a direct gain-controlled AKF without noise matrix iteration is designed to dynamically adjust Kalman gain via SMD, balancing static noise reduction and dynamic tracking. Moreover, the integrated adaptive processing suits both gyroscopes and accelerometers without separate calibration. Taking the gyroscope of the IMU as an example, in the 24-h outdoor static test, the proposed method reduces the time-domain variance from 28.664 ◦ /h to 2.297 ◦ /h, optimizes the bias instability (BI) from 1.033 ◦ /h to 0.493 ◦ /h, and improves the angular random walk (ARW) from 0.032 ◦ / boil √h to 0.017 ◦ / √h. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TC-SMD AKF in reducing the drift and random noise under static, dynamic, and long-term environmental conditions as compared with other existing algorithms.s.

title: Integration of BIM and Cloud-Based Tools for LEED Sustainable Building Design: A Case Study
authors_and_source: Chelaru B.,Ungureanu G., Onutu C. Buildings, 16(17), 3377
abstract: This research assesses the practical synthesis of Building Information Modeling (BIM), Autodesk Forma and Dalux to support LEED-oriented sustainable design for a higher education building. Autodesk Revit 2025 functioned as the central BIM platform, while Autodesk Forma enabled early-stage simulations of solar exposure, daylight potential, wind conditions, microclimate, noise and solar-energy potential. Dalux supported model coordination and information management in accordance with ISO 19650 principles. The workflow links simulation outputs to BIM elements through project-defined parameters, allowing performance evidence to inform design refinement. Quantitative indicators were consolidated for daylight exposure, wind comfort, outdoor thermal stress, acoustic exposure and photovoltaic potential. The solar-energy analysis considered an area of approximately 970 m , an annual potential of 1030 kWh/m and a theoretical yield of approximately 999,100 kWh/year. Assuming 70% roof coverage and 18% panel efficiency, the estimated photovoltaic the expected output is approximately 125,113 kWh/year. These findings demonstrate the value of combining BIM, cloud-based analysis and CDE-based coordination for early-stage sustainable design, while LEED certification, operational energy modelling and lifecycle assessment require additional specialist validation. The proposed workflow provides a consistent approach for aligning design development with sustainability objectives and can be applied to similar building types.

title: Three-dimensional thermomechanical analysis and performance assessment of an aluminum- lined, glass-fiber overwrapped hydrogen tank under hot-climate conditions
authors_and_source: Tiam Kapen P. Scientific African, 33, e03579
abstract: Hydrogen is increasingly central to decarbonizing transport and enabling long-duration energy storage, which places composite pressure vessels in harsh outdoor service. In sunbelt regions, tanks can face ambient temperatures approaching 50 °C together with intense solar irradiation, producing through-thickness thermal gradients that elevate liner temperature, modify composite response, and, when combined with internal pressure and cycling, reduce fatigue safety margins. However, many existing design and assessment studies assume near-isothermal behavior or consider thermal effects in isolation, limiting quantitative guidance for hot-climate deployment. This work presents a fully coupled three-dimensional thermo-mechanical finite-element analysis of a Type-III hydrogen tank (aluminum liner with glass-fiber/epoxy overwrap) using COMSOL Multiphysics 6.3. The model couples heat transfer in solids and gas with structural mechanics and imposes external convection-radiation, peak solar irradiance, and ambient temperatures up to 50 °C, together with internal hydrogen pressure and transient operating scenarios. Realistic solar exposure was achieved by computing the time-varying sun vector from the geographic coordinates of Maroua (Far North Cameroon) and applying it dynamically to the tank surfaces. Results showed pronounced vertical thermal stratification and crown-region heating, yielding an upper-dome thermal hotspot and circumferential stress bands peaking near 220 MPa (below liner yield), with predominantly radial displacements. Despite moderate stresses over most of the wall, fatigue damage localized near the lower outer shell/skirt junction, where geometric curvature and support constraints amplified the coupled thermo-mechanical stress range; the usage factor reached about 0.35 in this region while remaining below 0.1 elsewhere. Accordingly, the peak fatigue damage parameter increased from 0.291 under purely mechanical loading to approximately 0.35 ± 0.03 under coupled thermo-mechanical conditions. Importantly, this value represents the baseline environmental damage penalty per single 24-hour diurnal cycle rather than total cumulative lifetime damage, which will further accumulate under multi- cycle daily fast-refueling operations. To verify the framework’s numerical robustness against operational uncertainties, model credibility was evaluated through a reproducible measurement-emulation benchmark: synthetic sensor time series for crown gas temperature, maximum von Mises stress, and maximum displacement were generated by sampling the simulated signals and adding sensor-like noise and occasional outliers. The reconstructed 2 2 signals showed the lowest estimation errors (highest precision) for temperature and displacement, whereas peak- stress maxima exhibited higher dispersion, consistent with the sensitivity of extremum metrics to boundary-condition and property uncertainties. The study identifies the lower shell/skirt junction as the primary life-limiting region during hot-day cycling and motivates targeted mitigations such as local geometry smoothing, overwrap reinforcement, and thermal management to improve durability in hot climates.

title: Review of cross-modal and combined effects in real-world multi-domain outdoor environment on human responses
authors_and_source: Zhou H.,Wu Z. Building and Environment , 302, 114881
abstract: Outdoor human comfort is a key indicator for evaluating urban environmental quality, public health, and sustainable development. While individual environmental domains are well-studied, human perception is powerfully shaped by the interaction of multi-domain stimuli (thermal, acoustic, visual, and air quality). However, existing reviews have mainly focused on single-domain outdoor comfort, while evidence on interactions among multiple outdoor environmental domains remains fragmented and inconsistent, highlighting the need for an integrated framework for systematic synthesis. This review therefore aims to synthesize empirical evidence on cross-modal and combined effects in real-world multi-domain outdoor environments, clarify their influence on human responses, and provide an interpretive basis for understanding inconsistent and context-dependent findings. Using the PRISMA framework, this review synthesized 49 peer-reviewed empirical studies. Results confirm the thermal (94%) and acoustic (76%) domains as primary cornerstones, with the thermal–visual–acoustic triad (n = 16) being most prevalent. Overall outdoor comfort is governed by dynamic, non-linear and context-dependent mechanisms: thermal stress often acts as a “one-vote veto” factor under extreme climatic conditions, whereas acoustic quality becomes more influential under non-extreme conditions. Visual quality can provide aesthetic compensation, particularly for psychological restoration, while air quality remains insufficiently integrated into multi-domain models. Future research should strengthen cross-study comparability and integrate subjective, physiological, and modelling evidence to support more generalizable outdoor comfort assessment. This review deepens the understanding of interaction patterns among different outdoor environmental domains and provides a conceptual foundation for outdoor environmental design and urban planning.

title: Mechanical, acoustic, and thermal assessment of mortar embedded with polycarbonate particles obtained from end-of-life roofing sheets
authors_and_source: Li T.,Proietti M.G.,Nobili A., Moretti E. Construction and Building Materials , 534, 146908
abstract: The study investigates natural hydraulic lime mortar specimens in which polycarbonate (PC) particles obtained from milling end-of-life roofing sheets are used as a partial replacement of natural sand. Compared to plastics such as PET, PS and PVC, PC offers exceptional toughness, excellent heat resistance and transparency, as well as good dimensional stability. Since PC is susceptible to weathering, two types of PC waste are considered, which differ by the environmental exposure conditions during the service of the roofing sheets from which they were milled: indoor and outdoor, respectively. PC waste replaces natural sand (NS) at two replacement levels, and specimens are assessed in terms of mechanical, thermal, and acoustic performance. To better highlight the role of PC waste, comparison with control is carried out at different levels of water reducer addition (PCE) so that the same workability is achieved for all admixtures. Besides, to rule out the role of grading, PC particles are replaced by NS that has been sieved to match the grading curve of the plastic particles. In contrast to the general finding associated with plastic waste embedment, it is found that PC addition offers significant mechanical enhancement, both in flexure and in compression, in terms of ultimate strength, which increases by 20% (30%) at low (high) dosage; in terms of dissipated energy, which multiplies by 3–4 times over control; and in terms of failure mode, which transitions from brittle to ductile. Such outcomes appear consistently and are little sensitive to the PC type and to the PCE amount. Indeed, they seem associated with the flake shape of PC particles as well as with the peculiarities of PC. Specimen density is also reduced, which entails an improvement in terms of thermal conductivity that decreased from 0.69 W/(m·K) for the control mortar to 0.48 W/(m·K) at the highest PC content, corresponding to a reduction of about 30%. In contrast, acoustic absorption improved only for selected mixtures. Overall, results show promising potential for PC waste incorporation in mortar matrices, with significant benefits in the direction of waste reduction and reuse.

title: Differences in Multisensory Comfort Across Five Public Outdoor Functional Spaces: Evidence from an Autumn Field Study in Dalian, China
authors_and_source: Chen B.,Li X.,Deng S.,Li T., Zhang H. Buildings, 16(16), 3340
abstract: Outdoor comfort is influenced by thermal, visual, and acoustic stimuli, whose relative roles may vary across functional spaces. This study compared multisensory comfort characteristics across five frequently used public outdoor functional spaces in the main built-up area of Dalian, China, during the autumn transition season and examined their associations with overall comfort. Rotational fixed-point monitoring and synchronous questionnaire surveys were conducted in residential, cultural, educational, commercial, and green spaces, yielding 1497 valid responses. The results showed that: (1) Among the five investigated public outdoor spaces, the residential space had the highest proportion of positive overall comfort votes, whereas the educational space showed more thermal discomfort and negative acoustic evaluations. (2) Thermal and acoustic sensations changed linearly with corresponding exposures, while visual comfort first increased and then decreased with illuminance. (3) Thermal comfort had the largest main effect on overall comfort, visual comfort was also significant, and thermal–acoustic interaction was observed. (4) SEM indicated distinct association pathways. The thermal pathway showed a significant serial indirect effect through thermal sensation and thermal comfort, while the visual pathway contained indirect effects in opposite directions and the acoustic pathway was characterized mainly by a direct negative association between LAeq and overall comfort. These findings support function-sensitive multisensory assessment and targeted outdoor environmental optimization.

title: Net heat-flux measurement method for passive radiative cooling materials with ambient self- tracking
authors_and_source: Bertiglia F.,Forte D., Lopardo G.,... Fasano M., Pattelli L. Applied Thermal Engineering , 303, 132228
abstract: Passive Radiative Cooling (PRC) materials can efficiently dissipate thermal energy to outer space through the atmospheric window (8–14 μm), while reflecting most incident solar radiation, enabling sub-ambient cooling under direct sunlight. This work presents RAFT (Radiative Ambient-referenced Flux Testbed), a compact device for accurate outdoor PRC materials characterization. RAFT employs a heat flux meter to directly measure net heat flux, with the PRC sample mounted on the sensing surface and thermally coupled to an ambient-tracked reservoir via a compact fan-based convective heat exchanger integrated with heat pipes. Outdoor experiments demonstrated reliable ambient temperature tracking and accurate net heat flux measurements, which were further verified using an openly-released numerical model. Compared with conventional resistive heater-based outdoor setups, RAFT overcomes key limitations: it eliminates the need for feedback-control, shortens the measurement chain, reduces measurement noise when sample temperature approaches ambient, and enables quantification of both cooling and heating net fluxes with a total measurement uncertainty of ±1.8 W m . Relative to liquid-flow-based systems, RAFT offers improved portability and avoids the complexities of fluid handling. The proposed setup provides a robust and practical framework for outdoor evaluation of PRC materials, addressing the current lack of standardized protocols for direct heat flux measurement.

title: Experimental performance analysis of a realistic FSO link in weak turbulent channels for 5G backhaul connectivity
authors_and_source: Saeed S.,Khan A.N., Younis U. Journal of the Optical Society of America A Optics and Image Science and Vision , 43(8)
abstract: -2 Free-space optical (FSO) communication links have emerged as a promising solution for future networks such as 5G, 6G, and beyond by enabling low-cost, power-efficient, and high-speed backhaul connectivity. However, atmospheric turbulence can degrade link performance by reducing the optical signal-to-noise ratio (OSNR), increasing the bit error rate (BER) and limiting the achievable data rate. In this work, we employ a weak-turbulence channel model based on measured temperature and pressure to estimate the refractive index structure parameter (C ) and scintillation index ( σ ). These parameters are used to quantify turbulence strength and analyze its impact on optical beam propagation. The modeled OSNR and BER are analyzed for varying turbulence strengths. The measured OSNR of approximately 30 dB from the 50 m indoor channel corresponds to an achievable data rate of about 350 Mbps, yielding a BER of 10 , which is below the FEC threshold. The calculated OSNR is further validated using values derived from the measured received signal and noise optical powers. Finally, the (C ) value obtained from the indoor measurements is used to estimate the outdoor transmission range that provides comparable performance. The analysis predicts an effective outdoor link range of approximately 800 m, demonstrating the potential of this approach for designing FSO backhaul links in beyond-5G/6G microcell networks.

title: Soundscape diversity governs thermo- physiological and psychological states in a sexually dimorphic manner
authors_and_source: Tang Z.,Huang W., Zhang M.,Deng P.,Hong B. Building and Environment , 301, 114742
abstract: Although soundscapes modulate outdoor thermal perception, sex differences in physiological and psychological mechanisms under thermal stress remain elusive. This study examined thermo-acoustic interactions across six acoustic conditions that varied in diversity (low/medium/high) and environmental context (nature-dominant versus anthropogenic-dominant) in male and female participants exposed to graded thermal stress. Physiological indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, and eardrum temperature), electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, and psychological metrics were continuously monitored alongside microclimatic parameters. Results demonstrate marked sexual dimorphism in thermo-acoustic perception, primarily within nature-dominant environments. Males exhibited cardiovascular attenuation under slight thermal stress, with systolic pressure declining 6.08 mmHg (medium diversity) and diastolic pressure 6.61 mmHg (high diversity) versus low diversity (p < 0.05), though physiological responsivity diminished as thermal stress escalated. Females conversely demonstrated intensified physiological reactions with increasing thermal load, including reduced heart rate under no thermal stress conditions in anthropogenic settings (p < 0.05). In nature-dominant sound environments, low soundscape diversity attenuated male δ power while potentiating α power, consistent with diminished somnolence and heightened relaxation; elevated female θ power, conversely, indexed enhanced positive affect. Psychologically, males demonstrated consistently higher sensitivity, while females exhibited a biphasic pattern of initial attenuation followed by enhancement. In anthropogenic-dominant environments, males displayed heightened physiological and psychological sensitivity to acoustic diversity, whereas females showed asynchronous patterns: physiological responses weakened then strengthened, while psychological responses progressively intensified with increasing thermal stress. Our findings inform sex-sensitive acoustic optimization frameworks for urban design, advancing evidence-based healthy built environment strategies.

title: Critical analysis of smart materials in adaptive transparent systems for building façade
authors_and_source: Jaffar H.,Javed N.,Riaz A., ... Zhou C.,Zhang J. Energy and Environment , 37(5)
abstract: Adaptive transparent system (ATS) is an aspiring and effective building system that can adapt itself through environmental changes in spontaneous and reversible ways. It proposes an automatic and real-time response to indoor and outdoor conditions by increasing building energy efficiency and user comfort. This research presents a critical analysis to provide a preference order of the smart materials being used in the adaptive transparent systems. The approach of using smart material technologies in the building façades is discussed as the promising research direction for the future. A comprehensive literature review is conducted to identify the smart materials used in adaptive transparent systems along with their properties. Seven types of smart materials that are aerogel (AG), phase 2n I2 −8 2n change material (PCM), photovoltaic (PV), electrochromic (EC), thermo-chromic (TC), thermo-tropic (TT), and liquid crystal polymers (LCP) are selected based on evaluation criteria determined by the literature. The identified criteria are bulk density (BD), thermal conductivity (TCd), sound insolation (SI), fire retardation (FR), heat transfer coefficient (HTC), solar transmittance (ST), air purification (AP), annual energy saving (AES), cost saving (CS), ultraviolet (UV)/near infrared (NIR) control (UNC), and embodied carbon (EC). The identified seven smart materials are investigated with the help of two multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) techniques named analytical hierarchical process (AHP) and technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS) for analysis and ranking of materials. Results of the analysis demonstrate that PV is the most optimum material for adaptive transparent systems while others are ranked according to their performance.

title: Experimental investigation of synthetic jet– based active cooling for photovoltaic modules: Thermal management, acoustic characterization, and field validation
authors_and_source: Ghaly H.,Yakut K., Osta M.H. Applied Thermal Engineering , 302, 132025
abstract: The electrical efficiency and long-term performance of photovoltaic (PV) modules are adversely affected by heat accumulation within solar cells. Synthetic jet (SJ) actuators have emerged as a promising active cooling technology for PV systems due to their low power consumption and operation without an external fluid supply. However, the influence of nozzle geometry and outdoor performance of synthetic jet cooling on PV modules remain insufficiently investigated. In this study, 57-orifice synthetic jet actuators with nozzle geometries of 3, 5, and 7 mm were experimentally evaluated for PV thermal management. The effects of excitation amplitude, frequency, and orifice diameter on thermal and electrical performance were investigated under 1000 W/m solar irradiance. The optimal conditions were obtained at a 5 mm orifice diameter, 100 Hz frequency, and 3 V amplitude, resulting in a 16.5% reduction in average panel temperature and a 14.9% increase in maximum electrical power output. Outdoor experiments conducted in Erzurum demonstrated a reduction of up to 12 °C in surface temperature and a 7.5% increase in average electrical power output compared to the reference panel. Techno-economic analysis indicated a net annual energy gain of approximately 4.25%; however, the prototype-scale SJ system cost limited improvement in the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). The obtained results are competitive with water-based active cooling systems, which typically achieve 6–22% power gains but require continuous water supply and maintenance. Overall, synthetic jet-based cooling provides a water-free, low-power, and scalable thermal management solution for photovoltaic systems under realistic operating conditions.

title: Compact High-Performance Sensing Platform for Environmental Trace-Gas Monitoring Using MEMS-Based Thermal IR Detectors
authors_and_source: Venditti A.,Ayed F.B., Simeoni P.,Qian Z., Rinaldi M. IEEE Sensors Journal, 26(15)
abstract: This article reports the demonstration of a compact high-performance sensing platform for atmospheric trace-gas detection based on laser absorption spectroscopy (LAS). The proposed system integrates an infrared emitter, a Herriott cell, a thermal infrared detector, and a low-noise readout circuit, providing narrowband selectivity, high sensitivity, fast thermal response, and a compact form factor. The detector combines a piezoelectric laterally vibrating resonator (LVR) with a spectrally selective metasurface, enabling a responsivity of 0.65 Hz/nW and a thermal time constant of 2.3 ms. Since the extremely responsive and selective detection relies on a plasmonic metasurface with a lithographically tunable absorption peak in the mid-infrared spectral range, the signature absorption bands of common trace gas molecules can be matched and their detection targeted by properly selecting the emitter wavelength. Among those, nitrous oxide is used for a system-level validation due to its increasingly concerning impact as a greenhouse gas. Using a laser with emission wavelength near 4.53 μ m and an optical path length approaching 11 m, a sensitivity of 70.9 Hz/ppm is extracted. This corresponds to a limit of detection (LoD) of 14 ppb, considering the minimum Allan deviation of 1 Hz measured from the implemented readout circuit at an averaging time of 11 ms. The sensing platform is packed in a 3-D-printed housing with a total volume of 2 L and a weight of 800 g, suitable as a payload for integration with commercial drones. Preliminary robustness analyses and experimental 2 validation under vibration conditions further support the feasibility of the proposed system for outdoor drone-based operation.

title: Thermally stable GaN RF HEMTs on proton irradiated GaN substrates for low-noise applications
authors_and_source: Fan K.,Xu C.,Han J., ... Mao J.,Liu X. Applied Physics Letters , 129(4), 043502
abstract: In this study, proton irradiation is employed to fabricate semi-insulating GaN free-standing wafers with a sheet resistance of 5.9 × 10 Ω /sq. The mechanism for achieving semi-insulating GaN via proton irradiation is associated with the formation of a deep-level trap (E -0.54 eV), which is tentatively attributed to nitrogen antisite-related defects (N ). GaN-on-GaN high electron mobility transistors fabricated on the irradiated substrates exhibit stable operation over 300–375 K, with a minimum noise figure as low as 0.25 dB, with suppressed low-frequency noise characteristics. Additionally, the proton irradiation treatment GaN substrate also exhibits high volume production potential. This device is ideal for installation in harsh operational environments, such as satellite communication systems or outdoor base stations.

title: Phase Change Microcapsules Loaded in Polyurethane Foam for Dual-Purpose Thermal and Acoustic Insulation
authors_and_source: Zhu H.,Tan J.,Qiang X., Yin Y.,Wang C. ACS Applied Polymer Materials , 8(14)
abstract: Growing demand for lightweight and energy-efficient materials in building envelope systems has promoted the advancement of high-performance thermal insulation foams. Polyurethane foams (PUFs) are extensively adopted as porous insulation fillers owing to their low density, structural continuity, and suitability for scale construction deployment. However, insufficient skeleton strength and nonuniform pore size distribution limit the thermal insulation performance. In this study, n-tetradecane microcapsules were incorporated into a polyurethane raw material system, and phase change polyurethane composite foams (PCM-PUFs) were fabricated via a one-step foaming process. Microstructural characterization reveals that the composite foams exhibit a uniform closed-cell morphology, with the n-tetradecane microcapsules well dispersed and firmly embedded within the polyurethane cell walls; the average cell size is approximately 150 μ m. At an optimal microcapsule loading of 15 wt % and a corresponding encapsulation efficiency of 89.7%, the resulting PCM -PUF foam demonstrates substantially enhanced resilience and thermal buffering capacity. The support factor reaches 5.45, indicating excellent load-bearing capability and comfortability. The thermal conductivity is reduced to 0.05 W/(m·K). Under outdoor solar exposure, the surface temperature of PCM -PUF is 6.2 °C lower than that of neat PUF. Furthermore, PCM -PUF achieves an average sound absorption coefficient (AAC) above 0.9 and a noise reduction coefficient (NRC) exceeding 0.7, confirming that the incorporation of microcapsules does not compromise the sound insulation performance. The developed composite foam holds strong promise for building applications, particularly for regulating temperature fluctuations in scenarios with significant indoor–outdoor temperature differences.

title: Do we all feel the city the same way? A proof- of-concept framework linking physiological wellbeing to neighborhood-scale resilience through multi-domain environmental sensing
authors_and_source: Grapas C.,Schweiker M., Pisello A.L.,Pigliautile I., Cureau R.J. Building and Environment , 300, 114679
abstract: Outdoor comfort and climate adaptation studies usually focus on thermal-only investigations, typically relying on straightforward heat stress metrics. Human-centered validation frameworks to confirm whether built environment interventions reduce actual physiological stress versus predicted discomfort from population-averaged models still lack. To fill this gap, this proof-of-concept addresses three questions: (1) Do multi-domain environmental models explain physiological variance that thermal indices alone cannot capture? (2) Do individuals exhibit heterogeneous resilience to identical landscapes? (3) How can individual physiological data aggregate into neighborhood-scale 7 C Ga 15 15 15 resilience zones? Using synchronized wearable sensors (heart rate, electrodermal activity) and multi-domain environmental monitoring (Universal Thermal Climate Index, Particulate Matter, CO2, Acoustic Spectrum), we tested eight participants through contrasting Roman urban typologies such as exposed piazzas, tree-canopied riverbanks, enclosed gardens. Thermal comfort indices alone failed to predict stress, yet multi-domain models integrating thermal, air quality, and acoustic parameters explained up to 43% of physiological variance. Individuals with similar characteristics (age 28–38) and lifestyle exhibited markedly different physiological responses to identical microclimates, suggesting that the city is not felt the same way by everyone, and that population-averaged vulnerability models may not reliably predict individual-level stress outcomes. We operationalized three resilience metrics: Toughness, Recovery Capacity, Adaptation Duration, derived through generalized logistic growth modeling capturing nonlinear threshold dynamics in physiological stress responses. K-means clustering identified five statistically distinct adaptation zones corresponding to landscape typologies, demonstrating that individual wearable data enables neighborhood-scale resilience mapping. This framework establishes a preliminary methodological infrastructure for integrating physiological sensing with urban digital twins, enabling validation of whether landscape configurations reduce stress for inhabitants rather than relying on demographic prediction alone.

title: Research on Dual-Comb Ranging Technology Aiming at Space Applications (Invited) | 面向空 间应用的双光频梳测距技术研究 ( 特 邀 )
authors_and_source: Qin P.,Wang S. Zhongguo Jiguang Chinese Journal of Lasers , 53(14), 1404022
abstract: Objective Space-based high-resolution optical and radio imaging plays an irreplaceable role in geographic information resource acquisition, environmental monitoring, terrestrial planet searches and early-universe observations. In order to overcome the size limitations of single-aperture antennas, deployable antennas and distributed synthetic aperture imaging have become an emerging trend, which are all on account of high-precision absolute distance measurement. Optical frequency combs (OFCs) inherently generate equally spaced ultrashort pulse trains, corresponding to equally spaced phase-coherent spectral lines in the frequency domain. Such unique output signal enables not only high-resolution time-of-flight information but also high-accuracy interferometric data, which is ideal to reconcile the trade-off between dynamic range and precision in conventional ranging methods. Since the very beginning of the 21 century, high-precision distance measurements utilizing OFCs have been fully demonstrated with various distance calculation methods, comb structures, and ranging scenarios. On the other hand, space flights of simple OFCs have been reported by Korean and German groups, which illustrates the potential for space applications. However, complete space-borne comb ranging systems have not been reported until now. This research carries out systematic work from theoretical design to engineering optimization, and eventually accomplish an environmentally-stabilized fiber comb ranging system, which would lay the foundation of future space missions. Methods Firstly, a numerical model based on the split-step Fourier algorithm was established to systematically calculate the influence of the intracavity dispersion distribution on the timing jitter of the OFC oscillator. Concurrently, an all-polarization-maintaining fiber-based figure-9 cavity comb oscillator and a timing jitter measurement system based on optical cross-correlation were constructed, and an optical comb oscillator with low timing jitter was developed. Secondly, by utilizing a specially designed mechanical structure and adhesive bonding process instead of traditional mechanical mounts, a compact fiber-based OFC engineering prototype was developed. The prototype underwent environmental tests including vibration, acceleration, shock, thermal cycling, and thermal vacuum to verify its environmental stability. Thirdly, a fiber dual-OFC ranging engineering prototype was developed based on the OFC prototype. The accuracy and precision of its measurement results were experimentally verified with the indoor standard facility and the outdoor standard baseline at the National Institute of Metrology. Results and Discussions Firstly, through systematic numerical simulations, we found that to reduce the sensitivity of the timing jitter level to the uncertainty of intracavity net dispersion, it is necessary to achieve low timing jitter over a relatively wide range of net dispersion. This requires controlling the intracavity net dispersion to a near-zero, slightly negative value. Guided by the numerical simulation conclusions and combined with precise timing jitter measurements based on optical cross-correlation, we experimentally realized an all-polarization-maintaining figure-9 cavity OFC oscillator with high-frequency timing jitter of 93 as. Secondly, by employing structural and process designs, we developed an engineering prototype of the fiber-based OFC. After various environmental tests, the central wavelength and bandwidth of the oscillator’s output spectrum remained essentially unchanged, the signal-to-noise ratio of the radio st frequency spectrum consistently remained above 75 dB, and the amplifier output power and spectral shape were also maintained. These achievements ensure the stability of the OFC output signal from both theoretical and engineering perspectives. Thirdly, the dual-OFC ranging prototype underwent systematic experimental verification with standard distance facilities. The effective measurement range covered 0.99 to 432 m. The difference between the measurement results and the standard distance remained within the uncertainty of the standard distance throughout the entire range. The measurement accuracy reached the micrometer level, with the Allan deviation at one-second averaging time reaching 42.7 nm at 72.82 m and 63.8 nm at 432 m. Conclusions This research is based on the fundamental principles of OFCs, and covers a complete development process including numerical simulation, experimental verification, engineering prototype development, environmental test, and performance verification. It has preliminarily achieved the integration of theoretical design and engineering optimization, laying a solid foundation for the development and deployment of fiber-based OFCs and their high-precision ranging systems as space-borne payloads.

title: Quantum Reinforcement Learning for Air Conditioning Control Based on Variational Quantum Circuits
authors_and_source: Gandhi H.,Deng Z. Proceedings of the 16th ACM International Green and Sustainable Computing Conference Igsc 2026
abstract: We present a novel approach integrating quantum neural networks with reinforcement learning (RL) for house air conditioning control. Our framework employs a quantum deep Q-network (QDQN) RL implemented with PennyLane, leveraging parameterized variational quantum circuits (VQC) as function approximators for Q-values. The agent interacts with simulated indoor thermodynamic modelling, incorporating thermal capacity, heat transfer, and outdoor temperature variations. The action space consists of discrete air conditioning power levels, and the reward function balances comfort, energy, and switching penalties. To stabilize training, we introduce a target network, experience replay, and epsilon-greedy exploration. QDQN encodes the state vector into quantum rotations and applies multi- layer entangling gates, providing a potentially richer representation of the environment compared to classical networks. The QDQN agent uses VQC architecture. It incorporates data re-uploading, parameterized rotations, and strongly entangled qubits to effectively capture inter-feature correlations. We demonstrate the algorithm on episodes with outdoor conditions in both winter and summer conditions, showing convergence to policies that maintain indoor temperatures within setpoint bounds with zero violation rate. To validate the framework in a real-world noise setting, the quantum pipeline is simulated on the IBM Marrakesh system, featuring a 156-qubit Heron r2 processor with a median two-qubit (CZ) error of approximately 2.59 × 10 . Our results highlight the promise of quantum RL for real- world controls.

title: Possibility of using immersion cooling technology with virgin coconut oil for split-type AC
authors_and_source: Wibolo A.,Temaja I.W., Widiantara I.B.G., Arsana M.E.,Yusuf M. Sinergi Indonesia, 30(2)
abstract: Conventional split-type air conditioners are limited by high electrical consumption, noise from cooling fans, and bulky condenser coils that restrict installation flexibility. However, the application of immersion cooling in household AC systems remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the feasibility of using Virgin Coconut Oil (VCO) as a dielectric fluid for immersion cooling to improve energy efficiency and thermal performance. An experimental setup was developed using 20 L of SNI-compliant VCO, with the outdoor unit modified for immersion operation. Key performance parameters, including condenser coil and evaporator coil temperatures and the Coefficient of Performance (COP), were measured. Results showed condenser coil temperatures ranging from 40 °C to 58 °C and evaporator coil temperatures between 6 °C and 11 °C. The system achieved an average COP of 4.65 and reduced electrical consumption by approximately 20 %, indicating significant energy savings without compromising cooling efficiency. VCO also demonstrated suitable dielectric properties, with a breakdown voltage of 29.17 kV, near the IEC −3 156 threshold. These findings highlight immersion cooling with VCO as a promising, quiet, and energy-efficient alternative for household air conditioners. Further work is recommended to assess long-term reliability under varying operational conditions.

title: Interactive effects of noise and odor on construction workers' environmental perception and cognitive performance amid outdoor thermal stress
authors_and_source: Li Z.,Zhang X.,Peng Z., ... Li A.,Hong B. Building and Environment , 297, 114576
abstract: Construction workers chronically exposed to dynamic outdoor environments constitute a critical cohort for investigating multisensory environmental stress responses and cognitive ergonomics. This study systematically deconstructs the interactive effects of thermal stress gradients and noise–olfactory multimodal stimuli on workers' subjective thermal perception and neurocognitive performance in a cold region of China. Using a controlled field experiment with synchronized micrometeorological monitoring, we simultaneously acquired subjective environmental evaluations, multidimensional cognitive performance metrics, and electroencephalogram (EEG) data from 72 construction workers under nine factorial combinations of sound pressure levels (50/70/85 dBA) and odor types (Mentha piperita, Citrus sinensis, and Rosmarinus officinalis). A multidimensional benefit assessment model quantitatively ranked intervention efficacy. The results indicate that: (1) noise significantly modulated thermal sensation votes (p < 0.05), while thermal stress drove auditory sensation votes (p < 0.01). Neurophysiologically, escalating thermal stress enhanced low frequency ( δ ) activity and suppressed high-frequency ( α , β ) oscillations, with noise further diminishing frontal α -wave relative power (p < 0.05). (2) C. sinensis elevated significantly frontal-occipital θ -wave power (p < 0.05). (3) M. piperita broadly potentiated β -band activity under “neutral” conditions, yet R. officinalis yielded significantly lower thermal comfort votes than C. sinensis under “warm” conditions (p = 0.02). Our findings offer actionable climate adaptation frameworks for occupational health, safeguarding vulnerable workers against intensifying extremes in outdoor working environments.

title: Auditory comfort and noise perception under thermal and visual conditions in urban parks
authors_and_source: Simsek O. Scientific Review Engineering and Environmental Sciences , 35(2)
abstract: This study investigates auditory comfort in outdoor urban environments by examining the combined influence of visual and thermal factors. Field research was conducted in two major urban parks in Adana, Turkey, representing the Mediterranean climate, where simultaneous environmental measurements and surveys were performed during the autumn season. The collected data included air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, mean radiant temperature, sound pressure level, and both horizontal and vertical illuminance. Correlation and regression analyses revealed that sound pressure level was the most influential parameter, showing a strong negative association with auditory comfort, while higher vertical illuminance slightly decreased comfort levels. Thermal variables exhibited indirect effects on noise perception rather than on comfort itself. Participants expressed a strong preference for natural sounds such as birdsong and flowing water, while human and mechanical sounds were generally disliked. The findings highlight that auditory comfort is a multisensory phenomenon shaped by both acoustic and contextual environmental qualities.

title: Theoretical and experimental study of a novel thermoacoustic engine for sound source application
authors_and_source: Zhang L.,Kang H. Thermal Science and Engineering Progress , 74, 104699
abstract: This paper introduces a novel structures of standing-wave thermoacoustic engines designed for outdoor sound sources. The system is characterized by operational stability, enhanced SPL, and space-saving design. Compared to the conventional open-end system, the thin-plate sound source proposed is a closed-end one. The plate isolates the working gas from the external environment but remains acoustically transparent, enabling the use of alternative gases. Besides, it can effectively adjust the acoustic field distribution, enhance the acoustic power output. Experimental and theoretical research were conducted, the performance of systems using air or helium is analyzed and compared. The influence of thin plate properties on system behavior is investigated. Results show that with air as working gas, the system can achieve a higher SPL of 113.02 dB at 1 m away, marking a 5.4% increase in SPL compared to open-ended system. With helium adopted as the operational gas, the system can reach a highest SPL(1 m) of 123.49 dB with the condition of 0.3 mm SP and T = 675 K, indicating a 9.3% increase in SPL compared to system with air as working gas. The performance is significantly influenced by the thickness and Young's modulus. This system has potential for application as an outdoor sound source.

title: Quantifying outdoor thermal comfort in different street vegetation arrangements: Insights from a study in tropical and subtropical Australian cities
authors_and_source: Fu J.,Tavares S.,King D., Naylor S. Urban Climate, 67, 102967
abstract: Street vegetation serves as a nature-based strategy for urban heat mitigation leading to improved outdoor thermal comfort (OTC). A sound understanding of spatial and temporal OTC variation in different street vegetation arrangements is essential to strategically develop urban heat mitigation planning and design. This study introduces a methodology framework that quantifies the thermal improvement in different street vegetation arrangements by using three indices - cooling intensity (CI), cooling area (CA) and cooling duration (CD). The framework is applied to four streets in tropical and subtropical Australian cities to quantify Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) over a 24-h period. Results indicate that the street with trees on the west-facing side experienced a longer duration of street thermal enhancement (up to 38% CD improvement). During daytime hours, the OTC improvement in the planting scenarios with additional trees in the street centre (median strip) incorporating multiple vertical layers of vegetation is more pronounced in the studied subtropical urban area (up to 2.02 °C CI in Ipswich) than that in the studied tropical urban area (up to 1.03 °C CI in Townsville). These findings can contribute to urban heat mitigation planning and design in tropical and subtropical cities worldwide. The methodology framework proposed in this study provides a foundation for quantifying spatial and temporal OTC variation in different street vegetation arrangements, and establishes an adaptive framework for landscape architects, urban designers and planners, and decision-makers worldwide to evaluate urban street thermal environments.

title: Gas leak region recognition method constrained by gray-level statistical characteristics | 灰度统计特性约束的气体泄漏 区域识别方法
authors_and_source: Yang L.,Chen C.,Zhu T., ... Xiong W.,Lu J. Infrared and Laser Engineering , 55(5), 20250566
abstract: Infrared thermography plays an important role in gas leakage detection, and efficient detection algorithms are essential for enhancing practical applicability. This paper proposes a gas identification algorithm based on gray-level statistical features, which identifies anomalous regions through background modeling and chi-square statistics, and further confirms gas leakage regions using optical flow and morphological constraints. The results show that the false alarm rate is only 2.2% under no-leak conditions, with a processing time of 0.016 s per frame. For gas flow rates of 1 L/min, 3 L/min, and 5 L/min, the identification rates are 87.5%, 86.11%, and 99.07%, respectively, with an average processing time of 0.14 s per frame. The overall detection performance is satisfactory, and false alarms are effectively suppressed. The proposed algorithm does not require large-scale training datasets or precise environmental parameter modeling, while maintaining good generalizability, real-time performance, and ease of engineering deployment, offering an efficient and practical solution for gas leakage detection. Objective Accurate detection of gas leaks is essential for maintaining safety and protecting the environment in industrial and environmental monitoring h contexts. This study presents a robust and real-time method for gas leak detection utilizing infrared thermography. The proposed approach operates independently of large-scale labeled datasets and does not require physical models based on radiative properties, offering a generalizable and practical solution suitable for a wide range of monitoring scenarios. Methods A statistical and dynamic analysis approach is proposed. First, a background model is constructed from infrared video frames captured without gas release to obtain reference gray-level distributions. The overall gray-level deviation is quantified using the chi-square statistic to identify potential abnormal frames (Fig.3). The area of gas leakage is identified through pixel-level analysis using localized chi-square statistics computed over 5×5 neighborhoods. To reduce false positives, optical flow analysis is applied to verify the dynamic behavior of detected pixels, ensuring that only moving gas clouds are considered. In addition, constraints based on connected regions, including minimum area, shape compactness, and aspect ratio, are used to remove noise and pseudo- targets. Results and discussions Experiments were conducted in an outdoor simulated sulfur hexafluoride gas leak scenario at flow rates of 0, 1, 3, and 5 L/min. The results show that the proposed method achieves high detection accuracy and efficiency (Fig.4). The false-positive rate in the absence of gas is reduced to 2.2%, compared with 11.37% when using only global chi-square statistics (Tab.1 and Tab.3). For flow rates of 1, 3, and 5 L/min, the detection rates for identifying gas leakage areas are 87.50%, 86.11%, and 99.07%, respectively (Tab.3). Higher flow rates lead to improved detection because of stronger absorption and larger coverage areas. The average processing time per frame ranges from 0.01 s for non-leak frames to approximately 0.14 s for leak frames, demonstrating good real-time performance (Tab.3). The method reliably distinguishes gas leak regions from complex backgrounds and shows advantages in simplicity and generalizability compared with traditional statistical or physically modeled approaches. Limitations include occasional false positives caused by system noise, frame jitter, and dynamic environmental interference, as well as dependence on the quality of background modeling data. Conclusions The proposed method combines gray-level statistical analysis, dynamic verification, and region-based constraints to detect gas leaks in infrared thermal images. It achieves high detection accuracy, low false-positive rates, and real-time performance without requiring large training datasets or environmental parameter collection. Future work may incorporate additional image features, optimize optical flow parameters, and enhance background modeling to further improve robustness and reduce misclassifications in complex or dynamic environments. The method provides a practical and deployable solution for industrial and environmental gas leak monitoring.

title: Uncooled infrared spaceborne imaging method based on stop-and-stare scanning | 基于摆停 式扫描的非制冷红外航天成像方法
authors_and_source: Shen J.,Zhao J.,Wu W., ... Zhang Y.,Qi H. Infrared and Laser Engineering , 55(5), 20250529
abstract: Objective Uncooled infrared focal plane arrays (UFPA) have attracted extensive attention for small satellite thermal imaging missions because of their advantages of low cost, low power consumption, and the ability to operate without deep cryogenic cooling. However, their inherently limited thermal response speed and residual image effects under motion prevent UFPA from meeting the performance expectations of high spatial resolution spaceborne imaging systems. The objective of this research is to establish a systematic imaging method that reconciles ultra-wide swath coverage and image sharpness for UFPA-based payloads. This is achieved by extending the effective integration time of the detector during wide-area scanning, mitigating torque disturbances at the payload level, and improving geometric consistency for accurate multi-strip mosaicking and reliable detection of small-scale thermal targets such as wildfires. Methods A lightweight stop-and-stare scanning architecture is proposed, in which the scanning mirror alternates between rapid transition and short-duration dwell exposure phases, referred to as “fast transit” and “dwell exposure.” This segmented control of line-of-sight angular velocity allows the focal plane to acquire near-static exposure conditions within each dwell, effectively increasing the integration duration without enlarging the detector. To suppress nonlinear disturbance torques generated during the mirror motion, a payload-level angular momentum compensation system is designed using a counter-rotating flywheel driven by a stepper motor. The system operates in strict temporal synchronization with the scanning mirror, and an adjustable compensation coefficient ensures real- time balance between the two opposite rotational motions. For geometric accuracy, an analytic coordinate transformation framework based on the relationship between the satellite, the Earth, and the imaging plane is established to correct the geometric deformation of non-nadir remote sensing imagery and ensure consistency during strip mosaicking. The method was verified through multiple experiments, including dynamic MTF measurements using a gimbal–collimator–slit setup, single-axis air-bearing torque compensation tests, geometric correction using a blackbody calibration target, and outdoor wide-swath imaging and fire-point detection campaigns. Results and Discussions Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed method. The dynamic modulation transfer function (MTF) remains stably above 0.23, maintaining image contrast comparable to that of static imaging. The angular momentum compensation system reduces residual angular momentum from the order of 10 N·m·s to below 10 N·m·s, significantly lowering the disturbance transmitted to the satellite attitude control system. Geometric correction results show spatial deviations confined within 0.07 pixels, indicating accurate restoration of image scale and orthogonality. Field experiments confirm seamless image mosaicking across swaths exceeding 1000 km, while artificial 10-meter-class thermal fire points are clearly detected with a signal-to-noise ratio of 5.2 and sharp, point-like image features without visible trailing. These outcomes confirm that the proposed stop-and-stare scheme effectively trades scanning time for image sharpness, while the compensation mechanism ensures imaging stability. Together, these improvements provide a unified optical– mechanical–control solution for enhancing the clarity and consistency of wide-swath thermal infrared imaging using uncooled detectors. Conclusions The developed stop-and-stare scanning strategy, combined with an active payload- level angular momentum compensation device and an analytic geometric correction framework, effectively overcomes the conventional trade-off between swath width and image sharpness in UFPA-based spaceborne imaging systems. Quantitative experiments verify that dynamic MTF is sustained at or above 0.23, residual angular momentum is suppressed to the 10 N·m·s range, and geometric accuracy reaches sub-pixel level. Moreover, 10- meter thermal sources can be detected with high signal-to-noise ratio and geometric fidelity, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach. This study provides a practical, lightweight, and cost-effective solution for small-satellite thermal infrared missions and offers a new technical path for wide-swath, high-resolution imaging under dynamic conditions. Beyond its immediate engineering value, the work contributes theoretical and methodological support for future constellation-based fire monitoring, atmospheric thermal research, and intelligent spaceborne infrared observation systems, promoting long-term advancement in space infrared imaging technology.
